Orthopedics · published research

Heel pain

Some trials report reduced pain or improved activity, while systematic reviews find that results are not consistent for overall pain, function, or fascia thickness.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Some trials report reduced pain or improved activity, while systematic reviews find that results are not consistent for overall pain, function, or fascia thickness.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Pain > Heel pain category contains 29 unique titles: 21 human clinical reports and eight systematic reviews or meta-analyses. Reviews synthesize overlapping trials, and the clinical records include conventional PBM, high-intensity laser therapy, and combination regimens. These modalities and comparators should not be treated as one intervention.

Human and clinical evidence

In a 114-person randomized study, PBM added to usual care reduced pain and improved sports function compared with usual care (Ketz et al. 2024). A 69-person double-blind sham-controlled trial of red-light treatment also reported improvement in heel pain after six sessions over three weeks (Macias et al. 2015). However, the evidence is not consistent across outcomes or treatment types. A 2026 meta-analysis included 13 trials and 784 participants. It found improved heel tenderness but no significant pooled difference in overall pain, function, or plantar-fascia thickness; pain and function analyses were highly heterogeneous, and the review mixed lower-level and high-intensity laser studies (Ortiz-Romero et al. 2026).

Animal evidence

No animal study was identified in the exact heel-pain category.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo study was listed.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Conventional PBM trials use visible red or near-infrared laser, while high-intensity protocols use different power and delivery characteristics. The Macias trial used 635-nm red light at 17 mW for 600 seconds, with six sessions over three weeks. The Ketz trial evaluated PBM as an addition to usual care. Variation in diagnosis, co-intervention, and device prevents assuming that all laser results apply to low-level PBM.

Interpretation

Selected trials support short-term symptom improvement, but the evidence does not show a consistent effect across pain, function, and imaging outcomes.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term heel pain and function improvement with selected PBM protocols Very low for a uniform effect across devices and follow-up
Publications and records29 unique titles in exact Pain > Heel pain category

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The category contains 21 human publications and eight reviews, but trials mix conventional PBM with high-intensity laser and use varied comparators and schedules. Some direct trials report less pain or better function, while pooled findings are not consistent across outcomes. Replication with clearly specified modality and longer follow-up is needed.
